catalog_quote: [p. 11, sec. 2.1] Jamul exhibits the lexical structure and stress pattern typical of Yuman languages and described by Langdon (1975a: 219): A word contains a single stressed syllable, which may be surrounded by any number of unstressed syllables. Structurally, the word is composed of several layers of morphology. At the deepest layer is the morphological root. The root has the shape (C)V(C), where V stands for any vowel (short or long) and C for any consonant (including glides). The root contains the only stressed vowel of the word, and the terms stressed vowel and root vowel are used interchangeably. The root may be surrounded by any number of unstressed morphemes which together with the root form a meaningful unit called the stem. Inflectional morphemes are affixed to the stem, and syntactic prefixes and suffixes surround inflected stems. In general, prefixes outnumber suffixes by a w…
sweep_summary: kumi1248 (Tipai/Kumiai) is in the catalog as 'morphological' on Miller 2001 (Jamul Tiipay grammar, p. 11). this search of works with stress in the title had a single stress-title item, Gil Burgoin's 2016 El Colegio de México doctoral thesis on San José de la Zorra Kumiai; an open-access copy (CC BY-NC-ND) was already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 check and I re-read its stress chapter (sec. 4.2, pp. 178-183; sec. 4.3.2, pp. 226-227) and dialect placement (pp. 5-6, 14-15). It is squarely about word stress in this language and REFINES the catalog's classification: affixes never bear stress and the root keeps its stress under affixation (morphological), while within monomorphemic words stress is final in disyllables and penultimate in longer words, weight-insensitive, with an iambic OT analysis and acoustic correlates; the language is stated to be non-tonal. A line was added under Two extra sources seen in allowed trees: Mai, Aguilar & Caballero 2019 (JIPA, Ja'a Kumiai = kumi1248, held by the project in the ipai1240 folder) CONFIRMS root-coincident, predictable, morphologically conditioned stress that surfaces word-finally excluding enclitics; Langdon 1977 'Stress, Length, and Pitch in Yuman Languages' (SCOPIL 4) is print-only and unread (medium priority). Nothing found contradicts the classification. all judgements rest on the copies we hold and the bibliographic records in our check folders.

new_statements.quote: A partir de los datos presentados podemos hacer la generalización de que, si se toman en cuenta sólo las palabras monomorfémicas, el acento recae en la última sílaba en las bisilábicas y en la penúltima en las polisilábicas. Por otro lado, también es patente que los afijos no reciben acento y que, en el momento de la adjunción de distintos afijos, la raíz se queda con el acento que, normalmente, ocupa la misma sílaba en la palabra sin afijar que en la afijada.
new_statements.translation: From the data presented we can generalize that, if only monomorphemic words are taken into account, stress falls on the last syllable in disyllables and on the penultimate in polysyllables. On the other hand, it is also patent that affixes do not receive stress and that, when different affixes are attached, the root keeps the stress, which normally occupies the same syllable in the unaffixed word as in the affixed one.

new_statements.reading: A 295-page phonology dissertation with a 60-page chapter on word stress in the San José de la Zorra dialect of Kumiai (same glottocode as Jamul Tiipay; the author groups Jamul, San José de la Zorra and La Huerta together as southern Diegueño / Tipai, pp. 5-6). It agrees with Miller 2001 that stress is tied to the root and that affixes are never stressed (so the catalog's 'morphological' kind stands), and refines the description of where stress sits inside the root: final in disyllabic roots, penultimate in tri- and tetrasyllabic monomorphemic words, weight-insensitive, analysed as a right-aligned asymmetric iamb with NONFINALITY and *[AFFIX]; the language is not tonal, and stressed vowels are longer with a secondary pitch prominence on the final syllable of penult-stressed words. It does not supersede Miller 2001 as the deciding source: the catalog record is coded on the Jamul variety Miller describes, and Gil Burgoin's finding leads to the same coding; it should be added as a refining co-source (dialect-specific detail on non-final stress in longer roots).

new_statements.quote: All descriptions of Yuman languages agree that these are stress languages, and that stress is assigned morphologically to the root of the word. [...] Roots may function as words but more commonly words are formed by, among other processes, surrounding the root by prefixes and suffixes which produce unstressed syllables. Uninflected words tend to have stress on the last syllable in direct consequence of the great number of derivational prefixes and the very small number of derivational suffixes. [p. 239] [...] Note that regardless of the complexity of the word, the stress remains fixed on the root. [p. 240]

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog record (classification morphological, Miller 2001 p. 11: one stressed syllable per word, on the morphological root, all affixes unstressed, typically word-final because prefixes outnumber suffixes) — Miller's own passage cites Langdon (1975a: 219) for this typical Yuman pattern, and Langdon 1977 restates it for the whole family including Diegueño. Also consistent with the existing Gil Burgoin 2016 statement (affixes never stressed, root keeps its stress) and adds the compound secondary-stress detail. Identity caveat: Langdon's Diegueño examples are from the Mesa Grande dialect (Langdon 1970 grammar = Ipai, ipai1240), a sister variety; nothing in the paper is specifi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide statement covering Diegueño (Langdon's California-Delta group: Cocopa, Diegueño): every Yuman word has one stressed syllable, the root, and stress is assigned morphologically to the root, not by syllable count or weight; because derivational prefixes are many and derivational suffixes few (and usually a single consonant), uninflected words tend to come out with final stress, but syllabic (mostly syntactic) suffixes can follow the root, and the stress stays on the root whatever the word's complexity. Stress is a bundle of loudness, pitch and length (p. 240); vowel length is contrastive independently of stress; pitch is dependent on syllable configurations except in Kiliwa/Yavapai/Paipai/Mojave, which are discussed separately. Summary p. 252: 'Stress is basically morphological, it is a property of the root; length is contrastive in the manner of other segmental phonemes; and pitch is dependent on particular configurations of sequences of syllables in the word and in connected discourse, but has become contrastive in some languages.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 240: 'The only thing that can happen to a stressed syllable is that the stress reduces in compound formation to secondary stress on the first member of the compound, thus maintaining the preference for primary stress on the last syllable. Secondary stress in compounds may also further reduce so as to become indistinguishable from other unstressed material.' Diegueño examples xatapa: 'coyote' (xat 'dog' + pa: 'person'), matatay 'mountain' (mat 'ground' + tay 'big'). No rhythmic secondary stress described.
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 4 (p. 257): some investigators (Redden 1966 for Walapai, Halpern 1946-47 for Yuma) describe suffixes with primary stress so that some 'words' have two primary stresses; Langdon treats these as two words. Stress shifts off the root are reported only for Mojave (pp. 248-252, predictable from vowel length of pre-root and root syllables). For Diegueño (Mesa Grande dialect, pp. 241-242) she adds pitch facts: the stressed syllable is typically higher in pitch than the rest, unstressed syllables low except a pre-stress syllable with a long vowel or a vowel followed by glottal stop; Diegueño has neutralized the short/long contrast in roots ending in a vowel.
new_statements.identity_note: Langdon 1977 treats 'Diegueño' as one language of the California-Delta group (with Cocopa) and draws its Diegueño examples and pitch description from the Mesa Grande dialect (Langdon 1970 grammar), which Glottolog files as Ipai (ipai1240), a sister of Jamul Tiipay (kumi1248). The stress statement is explicitly made for all Yuman languages, so it covers Jamul Tiipay, but the paper does not describe the Jamul variety itself. Mojave, Kiliwa, Paipai, Yavapai and Walapai material in the paper concerns those other languages.

sources.citation: Mai, Anna, Andrés Aguilar & Gabriela Caballero. 2019. Ja'a Kumiai. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 49(2): 231-244.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: In Ja'a Kumiai, stress is similarly morphophonologically predictable: it coincides with the morphological root and supports phonological structures not found in other lexical positions, such as long vowels and complex consonant clusters, as also noted in Miller (2016a). The stressed syllable occurs word-finally excluding enclitics such as tag question marker [-ke'e] /=keʔe/ and demonstrative marker [-pe] /=pe/. Stress falls predictably and non-contrastively, so it is not considered phonemic in the language. However, since morphological structure is necessary to predict the location of primary stress, stress is notated on multisyllabic words in this description.
sources.note: Stress coincides with the morphological root (Miller 2001 / Langdon 1970 root), surfaces word-finally excluding enclitics, is predictable and non-contrastive, but morphological structure is needed to locate it; phonetically stressed vowels are ~2.2x longer and carry the amplitude and pitch maxima (p. 243). Supports the catalog's 'morphological' coding for a third dialect of kumi1248 (Ja'a, Baja California).
